title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can function as an automated teacher coach that provides useful classroom-observation feedback. The authors frame three coaching tasks for generative AI: (1) scoring classroom transcript segments using established observation rubrics, (2) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instruction, and (3) generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the NCTE Transcript dataset of U.S. elementary mathematics classrooms. It focuses on 4th- and 5th-grade transcripts from 317 teachers across four school districts, with expert human ratings from the CLASS and MQI observation instruments. ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) is evaluated zero-shot on quantitative score prediction and on qualitative feedback generation. For the qualitative tasks, experienced math teachers rate model outputs on relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, actionability, and novelty.

The main finding is that ChatGPT shows promise but is not yet reliable as a teacher coach. Its score predictions correlate weakly with human ratings, and adding rubric descriptions or chain-of-thought reasoning does not materially improve performance. For feedback generation, the model often produces responses that are relevant but not especially insightful, and a substantial fraction are unfaithful or redundant: many suggestions simply restate what the teacher already does in the transcript. The authors conclude that generative AI may eventually complement human coaching, but current systems need better grounding, novelty, and truthfulness before they can provide high-quality instructional feedback.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study with a clear evaluation design, but it is primarily a small-sample qualitative/benchmarking study using only two human raters and limited sampled transcripts. It lacks experimental causal identification and uses a narrow convenience sample, so it meets only limited credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not demonstrate educational gains; it documents model limitations and some qualitative promise for teacher coaching. Any practical impact is currently unclear and modest because performance is weak and the study does not show downstream benefits for students or teachers.

interventions.use_case: Zero-shot use of ChatGPT/gpt-3.5-turbo as an automated teacher coach to score classroom observation transcript segments, identify highlights and missed opportunities, and generate actionable suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning in elementary math classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether ChatGPT can reduce teacher-coaching workload by automating classroom observation feedback, but finds substantial limitations. Across 100 transcript segments, correlations with human ratings were low for all CLASS and MQI items (e.g., CLBM r=0.35 under direct-answer prompting; many others near 0 or negative), and teachers rated only 13-29% of outputs as faithful depending on task, indicating the system is not yet reliable enough to replace or substantially streamline expert coaching.
finding.measure: Spearman correlation with human rubric scores; teacher ratings of relevance, faithfulness, insightfulness, and actionability of generated feedback
finding.study_size: n=100 for scoring; n=216 CLASS items, n=288 MQI items for highlights/missed opportunities; n=36 suggestions

finding.finding_summary: For elementary math instruction transcripts, ChatGPT showed limited ability to score math instruction quality and provide useful math-teaching feedback. In Task A, correlations with MQI scores were low overall (EXPL r=0.02, REMED r=0.05, LANGIMP r=0.00, SMQR r=0.17 under direct-answer prompting), and in Task C the model’s suggestions were often actionable and faithful but redundant 82% of the time, repeatedly describing what the teacher already did rather than offering novel guidance.
finding.measure: Human-rated MQI observation scores and teacher ratings of math-specific feedback quality
finding.study_size: n=100 for scoring; n=288 MQI items for qualitative evaluation; n=36 suggestions
finding.effect_size: Spearman r values: EXPL 0.02, REMED 0.05, LANGIMP 0.00, SMQR 0.17 (DA); redundancy 82%
